entries.clue: Best unfashionable educational unit (8)

blocks.note: what is out has gone out of fashion
a class is the unit a school timetable is cut into

annotation.surface: Someone is picking the finest of a school's dowdiest teaching groups.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Best' is a verb here, to beat, and not the superlative adjective the surface offers. 'Out' for unfashionable is a staple that opens dozens of answers.
annotation.definitionFit: To best a rival is to beat them decisively, and the answer is the plain verb for beating them so far they are in another league.

entries.clue: (&28ac.) Lawless, moody, stupid old fascist (6)

indicatorNotes.stupid: A stupid arrangement is one nobody would have chosen, so the letters in front are not standing in the order that works.

blocks.note: twelve letters for the pile, wanted for their spelling rather than their sense

annotation.surface: A sketch of a thuggish, sulking, dim figure from the past.
annotation.walkthrough: Three insults in a row, and only the third is an instruction — the first two are raw material. The cross-reference matters: twelve letters are wanted, spread over two entries.
annotation.definitionFit: Sir Oswald Mosley founded the British Union of Fascists and led its blackshirts through the 1930s, so 'old fascist' names him by his politics and his date.

entries.clue: "FAKE, EXCESSIVE, BACKWARD" is rather shrill (8)

indicatorNotes.BACKWARD: Something backward faces the way it came from, so the piece just named is written out from its last letter to its first.

blocks.note: a fake signature is a false one
OTT is 'over the top', the everyday shorthand for excessive

annotation.surface: A blurted verdict on somebody — fake, over the top, behind the times.
annotation.walkthrough: The capitals are a trick of the eye, making three words look like a quoted slogan when two are fodder and one is an instruction. OTT for excessive is the piece to keep.
annotation.definitionFit: Falsetto is the strained register above a man's natural range, and it comes out thin and piercing — shrill without being a shriek.

entries.clue: One who winds up getting arse thrashed after the election starts (6)

indicatorNotes.thrashed: A thrashing leaves what it lands on in no fit state, and letters in that state will not stay in the order handed over.
indicatorNotes.after: What comes after something is written behind it, so the shuffled four follow the pair taken from the election.
indicatorNotes.starts: A start is where a thing begins, so only the opening letter of each word in front of it is taken.

blocks.note: the opening letters of 'the' and 'election'
four letters for the pile, wanted for their spelling

annotation.surface: Somebody is getting a beating on the backside now the campaign has begun.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Winds up' is the British sense of needling a person until they snap, not the clockwork or the finishing sense. Two words share one instruction, which is why 'the election starts' reads as plain reportage.
annotation.definitionFit: A teaser is the one who provokes others for sport, the person sense of the word rather than the puzzle or the trailer.

entries.clue: Old banger's heavenly belt (6)

blocks.note: the reading the surface pushes: a clapped-out car held together by hope
the reading the setter means: a band drawn across the sky

annotation.surface: A worn-out car is said to own a belt from the heavens.
annotation.walkthrough: The Ford Zodiac was a big British saloon of the 1950s and 60s, which is how a car name reaches the sky. A possessive apostrophe is all that joins the two senses.
annotation.definitionFit: A Ford Zodiac is the sort of car that ends up an old banger, an example standing for the class; the zodiac itself is the sun's belt of sky.

entries.clue: Coalition parties' leaderless flirtation (8)

indicatorNotes.leaderless: A body with no leader has lost the one at its head, so the word it governs goes without its first letter.

blocks.note: a dalliance is a flirtation, a light affair nobody means to last
the letter standing at the head of that nine is the one dropped
the possessive belongs to the surface picture and puts in no letters

annotation.surface: Political parties are flirting with each other while nobody is in charge.
annotation.walkthrough: One letter off the front of one word does the whole job, which is why the clue looks too short to contain wordplay. 'Parties' is dressing: it makes the sentence a sentence and nothing more.
annotation.definitionFit: An alliance is a formal joining of forces, and when parties do it in a parliament the newspapers call the result a coalition.

entries.clue: To adhere to lockdown rules, possibly is to shatter sanity! (4,2)

annotation.definition: To adhere to lockdown rules, possibly

indicatorNotes.shatter: Shattering a thing leaves its pieces in any order at all, which is what becomes of the letters that follow.

blocks.note: six letters for the pile, wanted for their spelling

annotation.surface: Obeying the lockdown rules is what sent everybody out of their minds.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' is doing definition work rather than anagram work: it concedes that this is one way of obeying the rules, not the only one. Fodder and answer are cause and effect, which is the joke.
annotation.definitionFit: To stay in is to remain indoors, which is what the lockdown rules demanded — an example of obedience rather than a synonym for it.

entries.clue: Not fully satisfied about Farage finally thrown out of parliament? (8)

indicatorNotes.about: To put one thing about another is to wrap it round, so the longer piece closes over the letter that follows.
indicatorNotes.finally: Finally points at where a word ends, so its last letter is all that is taken.

blocks.note: an appetite left unmet is unsated
the last letter of the surname

annotation.surface: Somebody still hungry is grumbling about Nigel Farage losing his Commons seat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' reads as 'concerning' and is really the instruction to wrap one piece round another. The trap is waiting for Farage to supply a chunk; he supplies one letter.
annotation.definitionFit: An MP who loses their seat is unseated, the word Westminster uses for being turned out of the House.

entries.clue: Overturned toilet – hindrance or aid to the drinker? (6)

indicatorNotes.Overturned: An overturned thing has been tipped end over end, so the word it governs is read from its last letter back to its first.

blocks.note: the bog is British slang for the lavatory, here tipped upside down
a let is an obstruction in law and in tennis, as in 'without let or hindrance'

annotation.surface: A lavatory has been knocked over, and a drinker wonders whether that helps.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Let or hindrance' is the legal phrase the clue quietly quotes, and it splits down the middle: one word is wordplay, the other is not. The drinker of the surface is drunk; the drinker of the definition just wants a cup.
annotation.definitionFit: A goblet is a stemmed drinking cup, so it is literally the thing that helps a drinker get the drink down.

entries.clue: People causing stink with abrupt response (6)

indicatorNotes.abrupt: An abrupt reply is one cut short, so the word for a reply is written in its clipped form.

blocks.note: to hum is British slang for to smell strongly
the three letters a form cuts an answer down to

annotation.surface: Troublemakers kick up a fuss and snap at anyone who objects.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stink' is the fuss you kick up in the surface and the smell you give off in the wordplay. A definition this wide gives no help at all, which is the point of using it over two short pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: People is the everyday plural for members of our species, so it swaps straight in without any stretch.

entries.clue: (& 12ac.) What many of Trump's actions amount to? US districts pay off (5)

annotation.definition: What many of Trump's actions amount to?

indicatorNotes.off: Something gone off is no longer in the state it was sold in, and letters that have gone off will not keep the order given.

blocks.note: fourteen letters for the pile, wanted for their spelling rather than their sense

annotation.surface: American constituencies are quietly handing money over to somebody.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pay off' reads as one phrase, a bribe, and the clue splits it so that only the last word gives an instruction. The question mark admits the definition is a verdict rather than a dictionary sense.
annotation.definitionFit: Crass stupidity is coarse, unthinking folly, and the clue offers that as the sum of those actions — an opinion the question mark owns up to.

entries.clue: see 11ac.
One making financial checks on inept, asinine leaders' conference venues? (9)

indicatorNotes.leaders': A leader stands at the front, so what is taken is the front letter of each word before it.

blocks.note: an auditor is the person who inspects a company's accounts
the opening letters of the two insults

annotation.surface: An accountant goes through the books of hopeless heads of state at their summit.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe lets 'leaders' be a possessive in the surface and an instruction in the wordplay at the same time. Auditoria is the Latin plural that theatres and publishers still prefer to auditoriums.
annotation.definitionFit: Auditoria are the halls where an audience sits, which is where a conference seats its delegates — a plural definition for a plural answer.

entries.clue: Law of prison taking negative turn (5)

indicatorNotes.turn: To give a thing a turn is to swing it round to face the other way, so the word before it is read from its end back to its start.

blocks.note: the can is slang for jail — a spell inside is time in the can
the two-letter refusal, before anything is done to it

annotation.surface: The rules of a jail are being changed for the worse.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Law of prison' invites you to look for a prison sense in the answer, and the prison belongs to the wordplay instead. A two-letter negative swung round is among the oldest moves in the grid.
annotation.definitionFit: A canon is a body of law or a settled rule — canon law being the church's own legal code — so the flat word covers it.

entries.clue: Drug-taking senior with debts that will lead to grave (7)

indicatorNotes.taking: A person taking a drug has it inside them, so the letter for the drug is planted inside the word alongside.

blocks.note: Sr is the senior on a nameplate, distinguishing father from son
E is ecstasy, the crossword's default drug
an IOU is a written debt, and here there is more than one

annotation.surface: An elderly addict is in over his head with money he owes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Grave' looks like the noun the surface is heading for, the hole in the ground, and it is the adjective. The hyphen in 'Drug-taking' hides a seam: one half names a letter, the other says where to put it.
annotation.definitionFit: A grave error and a serious error are the same error — both words mean weighty enough to worry about.

entries.clue: Furious-looking, mad wartime medics (3,5)

annotation.definitionNote: The answer is one organisation and 'medics' is plural, but the name is routinely used for its people in the field, the way 'the fire brigade' stands for the crew who turn out.

blocks.note: a face gone red with rage looks furious
cross is the mild British word for angry, the one used to children

annotation.surface: Red-faced, bad-tempered doctors somewhere in a war.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves mean angry, which is why the clue reads as one idea instead of two pieces laid end to end. 'Mad' is wanted for the annoyed sense, not the insane one.
annotation.definitionFit: The Red Cross is the international relief organisation whose emblem the wounded look for, and whose volunteers have treated battlefield casualties since 1863.

entries.clue: Wicked Paris with large behind, producing wind (6)

indicatorNotes.Wicked: A wicked person is crooked, bent out of true, and letters bent out of true come out in another order.

blocks.note: five letters for the pile — the Trojan prince or the city, it makes no difference
L is the large on a clothing label, joining at the back of the pile

annotation.surface: A disreputable Parisian with a big bottom is breaking wind.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wind' is the crude noun the surface wants and the verb the definition needs, the one that rhymes with 'find'. 'Large behind' does two jobs in two words: the letter, and where it goes.
annotation.definitionFit: To spiral is to wind — what a staircase or a climbing vine does, turning round a centre line as it rises.

entries.clue: Merger of the Sun and Express, which some might sniff at (7)

indicatorNotes.Merger of: A merger makes two bodies into one, so the two pieces named are run together into a single word.

blocks.note: Sol is the Latin name for the sun, still used for our own star
to express anger is to vent it

annotation.surface: Two British tabloids, the Sun and the Express, merge into a paper snobs would despise.
annotation.walkthrough: Capital letters turn a star and a verb into two newspapers, and that is the whole misdirection. 'Sniff at' means to look down on in the surface and to inhale in the definition — glue, not snobbery.
annotation.definitionFit: Glue, thinners and lighter fuel are solvents, and their fumes are what solvent abusers inhale, so the definition names the answer by the way it is misused.

entries.clue: Spoiled duke screwed off balance (8)

indicatorNotes.screwed: A screwed-up sheet of paper has lost every bit of its shape, and letters treated that way come out in a different order.

blocks.note: seven letters for the pile, wanted for their spelling
D is the duke of a peerage list

annotation.surface: A pampered aristocrat, drunk and unable to stand up straight.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spoiled' looks like the adjective describing the duke and is the raw material; 'screwed' looks like his condition and is the instruction. D for duke comes off the same peerage list that gives E for earl.
annotation.definitionFit: Something lopsided carries more weight on one side than the other, which is what being off balance looks like from outside.

entries.clue: Subject: "Aid rejected" – slated by Trump (3,5)

annotation.definitionNote: This definition points rather than substitutes: instead of a synonym it names its answer by who is forever attacking it, which is how a solver is meant to recognise it.

indicatorNotes.rejected: To reject a thing is to throw it back, so the three letters in front are written back to front.

blocks.note: the subject of an essay is its theme
help thrown back the way it came

annotation.surface: An email headed "Aid rejected" has drawn an attack from Trump.
annotation.walkthrough: The colon and the quotation marks dress the clue as a memo, and neither piece of punctuation carries an instruction. 'Slate' is British for to criticise savagely, the sense a tabloid headline uses.
annotation.definitionFit: Press and broadcasters together are the media, and they are the standing target of Trump's abuse.

entries.clue: Music's accepted decline? (5)

blocks.note: a person who is in has been accepted by the group
a wind or a fire that declines dies away

annotation.surface: The slow fading of a style of music everybody once welcomed.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark is earning its keep: what is wanted is one genre, not music in general. 'In' for accepted is the same 'in' as the in-crowd.
annotation.definitionFit: Indie is the guitar music made outside the big labels, so the bare word 'Music' defines it by its category, one kind standing among many.

entries.clue: Revenue generated by hot orgasm (6)

blocks.note: what is hot just now is in, the fashionable choice
the blunt verb for reaching a climax, taken as a noun

annotation.surface: Money is being made out of steamy sex.
annotation.walkthrough: The smut is the misdirection and not the mechanism: both pieces are ordinary words and the second is merely crude. 'Hot' for 'in' is the fashion sense, as in a hot ticket.
annotation.definitionFit: Income is the money coming in over a period, which is what revenue means on any set of accounts.

entries.clue: It can hit ships once round about eastern end of strait (6)

indicatorNotes.end of: The end of a word is its final letter, so that single letter is all the word that follows gives up.

blocks.note: ex- means former, as in an ex-wife
the letter drawn as a circle
c is circa, the 'about' put in front of a date
E is east on any compass
the last letter of the narrow channel

annotation.surface: Something once circled the eastern mouth of a strait and could sink what passed.
annotation.walkthrough: Five tiny pieces in a row and no pile to shuffle — the difficulty is that every small word is quietly working, 'round' and 'about' included. Exocets were the French missiles that sank British ships in the Falklands in 1982.
annotation.definitionFit: The Exocet is a French sea-skimming anti-ship missile, built for precisely the job the definition describes.

entries.clue: Pissed sailor snuggles into awfully nice lap (9)

indicatorNotes.snuggles into: To snuggle into something is to settle down inside it, so the sailor's letters sit within the pile once it has been shuffled.
indicatorNotes.awfully: Awfully is the schoolroom's 'very badly', and letters handled very badly end up in the wrong order.

blocks.note: seven letters for the pile, wanted for their spelling
an AB is an able seaman in the Royal Navy

annotation.surface: A drunken sailor curls up in somebody's comfortable lap.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Awfully nice' reads as one polite phrase and the clue splits it, leaving the first word as the instruction. The sailor goes into the shuffled letters, not into 'nice lap' as it stands.
annotation.definitionFit: Pissed is British for drunk, and 'drunk and incapable' is the charge-sheet phrase where the answer carries that sense on its own.

entries.clue: Chlorine always makes you smart (6)

blocks.note: Cl is chlorine's symbol on the periodic table
ever means always, as in ever-present

annotation.surface: The chemicals in a swimming pool are sharpening your wits.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Smart' is the sting the surface promises, since chlorine makes the eyes smart, and the definition wants the other sense entirely. Chemical symbols are fair game anywhere in a cryptic.
annotation.definitionFit: Smart and clever are the same adjective for quick-witted, the sense in 'a smart answer'.

entries.clue: Live with a Tory? Danger alert! (6)

blocks.note: to live is to be, as in 'let it be'
the article taken as a single letter
Con is the British ballot paper's abbreviation for a Conservative candidate

annotation.surface: Sharing a house with a Conservative counts as a warning sign.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Live' reads as the adjective, as in a live wire, and is the verb. Con for Conservative comes off ballot papers and election-night graphics, where Lab and Lib Dem sit beside it.
annotation.definitionFit: A beacon is a fire or light set on a hill to warn of invasion, so raising an alert about danger is its entire purpose.

entries.clue: (& 27ac.) Nasty ICE operator impounds a periodical – which multinationals try to present in a good light (9)

annotation.definition: which multinationals try to present in a good light

indicatorNotes.Nasty: Something nasty has turned bad, and letters that have turned bad will not stay in the order they were given.
indicatorNotes.impounds: To impound a thing is to take it in and hold it, so the shuffled letters close round what comes next.

blocks.note: ICE is the United States immigration enforcement agency, and its eleven letters are the pile
a mag is a magazine, a title that comes out at fixed intervals

annotation.surface: A brutal immigration officer confiscates somebody's magazine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'ICE operator' reads as a job rather than eleven letters, which is how a pile that long hides in plain sight. The definition describes what the answer is for instead of what it means, and runs on into 27 across.
annotation.definitionFit: A corporate image is the impression a company works to project, which is exactly what a multinational's public-relations budget exists to keep flattering.

entries.clue: see 26ac.
see 2dn.
"Hot stuff" Penny grabbed by Lords member, perversely in love (8)

indicatorNotes.grabbed by: Being grabbed by somebody leaves you in their hands, so the letter in front goes inside the word that follows.
indicatorNotes.perversely: Perverse means turned the wrong way about, so the two small pieces just named are read back to front.

blocks.note: a peer is a member of the House of Lords
p is the penny on a British price tag
the word itself, taken for its two letters
love is nothing in tennis, and nothing is the round letter

annotation.surface: A peer has got hold of a woman called Penny and is thoroughly smitten.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Penny' looks like a name and is the coin. The letter count rules out the doubled p of the usual English spelling, leaving the Italian one.
annotation.definitionFit: Peperoni is the fiery cured sausage off the pizza menu, so 'hot stuff' is its taste as much as the come-on the surface intends.
